Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> Opinion Ghana’s Education Crossroads: Why Artificial Intelligence must become a tool for inclusive learning and national transformation Source : Madeleine Insaidoo 20 November 2026 6:45pm ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
As Ghana prepares to mark National Education Week 2026 on November 23 and 24, attention is increasingly turning to the role artificial intelligence (AI) can play in shaping the future of education. But beyond the excitement surrounding this emerging technology lies a more important question: How can AI improve learning, empower teachers and ensure that no Ghanaian child is left behind?
Ghana's education system is at a defining moment. The world of work is changing, new industries are emerging, and the skills required to participate meaningfully in the global economy are extending beyond traditional academic knowledge. Digital competence, critical thinking, creativity, problem-solving and the ability to work with emerging technologies are becoming increasingly important.
Artificial intelligence is at the centre of this transformation. Already, it is changing how people access information, communicate, conduct research and solve problems. For Ghana, the challenge is no longer whether AI will influence education, but how effectively the country can harness its potential while addressing the risks and ensuring that its benefits reach every learner.
It is against this background that the Ministry of Education is organising National Education Week 2026 under the theme, " Harnessing Artificial Intelligence for Inclusive and Transformative Education in Ghana ."
Scheduled for November 23 and 24, 2026, at the Ghana Tertiary Education Commission (GTEC), the event will bring together policymakers, educators, researchers, students, development partners, technology experts and other stakeholders to examine how Ghana's education system can respond to the opportunities and challenges presented by AI.
More importantly, the event provides an opportunity to move the conversation beyond simply introducing technology into classrooms and focus on how it can improve the quality, relevance and inclusiveness of education.
In his 2025 State of the Nation Address, President John Dramani Mahama emphasised the need for Ghana's education system to respond to the demands of the 21st century and the Fourth Industrial Revolution.
That call reflects the urgency of the moment. For many years, education has largely focused on the transfer of knowledge from teachers to learners. While this remains fundamental, the changing world requires an education system that also equips learners to question information, think independently, apply knowledge and adapt to new circumstances.
Artificial intelligence offers opportunities to support this shift.
In the classroom, AI-powered applications can help teachers identify areas where learners are struggling, provide additional explanations and tailor learning experiences to individual needs. Students can also access educational resources and explore difficult concepts with greater flexibility.
Teachers, on the other hand, can use AI to support lesson preparation, develop teaching materials, assist with assessments and identify learning gaps. School administrators can benefit from data-driven systems that strengthen planning, monitoring and decision-making.
At the tertiary level, AI offers opportunities to advance research, encourage innovation and strengthen collaboration between academic institutions and industry.
However, the success of this transformation should not be measured by the number of digital devices distributed to schools or the sophistication of the software introduced. What matters most is whether these investments translate into better learning outcomes, expanded opportunities and improved preparation for life and work.
As Ghana considers the integration of artificial intelligence into education, inclusion must remain a central concern.
Technology has the potential to open up new learning opportunities, but without deliberate planning, it could also widen existing inequalities.
A learner in an urban school with reliable internet connectivity, access to digital devices and digitally competent teachers may enjoy far greater benefits from AI-supported learning than a child in a rural community where electricity, connectivity and educational resources remain limited.
The needs of learners with disabilities must also receive particular attention.
AI-enabled accessibility tools, including speech-to-text applications, text-to-speech systems, automated captioning and adaptive learning platforms, can help remove some of the barriers that prevent learners with diverse needs from participating fully in education.
However, making these opportunities available will require investment in accessible infrastructure, appropriate learning materials and teacher capacity development.
The objective must be to prevent AI from becoming another dividing line between well-resourced and underserved schools. Instead, it should serve as a means of narrowing educational inequalities and extending quality learning opportunities to communities across the country.
This is particularly important for Ghana's national development aspirations, which depend on equipping every child, irrespective of geographical location, economic circumstances or physical ability, with the knowledge and skills to contribute meaningfully to society.
One concern surrounding the growing use of artificial intelligence in education is whether technology will eventually reduce the importance of teachers.
Although AI can process information, generate explanations, identify patterns and provide learning support, teaching involves much more than delivering information. Teachers inspire curiosity, build confidence, encourage discipline, provide emotional support and recognise the individual needs of their learners. They also play a critical role in nurturing the values, judgement and social skills required to develop responsible citizens.
These human dimensions of education cannot simply be replicated by technology.
Rather than viewing AI as a replacement for teachers, Ghana must position it as a tool that strengthens their professional capabilities and gives them additional resources to support learning.
Achieving this will require continuous professional development to help teachers understand how AI works, use it effectively and recognise its limitations. It will also demand changes in teaching approaches, with greater emphasis on critical thinking, creativity, independent inquiry and the responsible use of information.
Ultimately, the success of AI integration will depend as much on the preparedness of teachers and other education professionals as it will on the availability of technology.
Ghana is not starting this journey from scratch. The country has already taken steps towards building a digital economy in which artificial intelligence can contribute meaningfully to national development.
In April 2026, President John Dramani Mahama launched Ghana's National Artificial Intelligence Strategy, covering the period 2025–2035. The strategy identifies education, human capital development, research, ethical AI development and workforce readiness as important areas of focus.
Government also announced plans for a US$250 million Artificial Intelligence Computing Centre to support research, innovation and the development of local AI solutions. These initiatives reflect the country's ambition to move beyond merely consuming technology towards building the capacity to develop solutions that respond to its own needs.
Within the education sector, there are equally significant developments.
In May 2026, the Ministry of Education signed a Memorandum of Understanding with Google for Education to strengthen digital literacy and support the integration of advanced AI technologies into teaching and learning. The partnership is expected to contribute to teacher development, classroom innovation and the acquisition of relevant skills by Ghanaian learners.
Another important development is the proposed revision of the basic school curriculum from Kindergarten to Primary Six. Presented to the Minister for Education in July 2026, the revised curriculum incorporates artificial intelligence literacy, computational thinking, coding and digital citizenship, alongside other proposed changes.
These additions reflect a growing recognition that learners must begin developing an understanding of technology and its applications from an early age. The curriculum review also recommends a phased and adequately resourced teacher-training programme to support implementation.
The Centre for National Distance Learning and Open Schooling (CENDLOS), which provides leadership in open, distance and electronic learning, also has an important role in expanding technology-enabled learning opportunities.
Together, these initiatives provide a foundation for the discussions expected at National Education Week 2026.
The task ahead is to ensure that these efforts are properly coordinated, adequately resourced and translated into practical improvements across schools and other educational institutions.
While the opportunities presented by artificial intelligence are considerable, embracing the technology without addressing its risks could undermine the very objectives the education sector seeks to achieve.
Unequal access remains one of the biggest concerns. AI-supported learning cannot become a national solution if large numbers of learners and teachers lack electricity, reliable internet connectivity, appropriate devices and the skills required to use them.
Other concerns include data privacy, cybersecurity, algorithmic bias, misinformation and the reliability of information generated by AI systems.
There is also the danger of excessive dependence on AI-generated answers. Without proper guidance, learners may become less inclined to conduct independent research, question information or develop their own ideas.
Academic integrity presents another important challenge. Educational institutions will need clear guidelines on the acceptable use of AI in assignments, examinations, research and other academic activities.
Beyond these concerns is the question of relevance. AI systems developed in other parts of the world may not always reflect Ghana's educational environment, indigenous languages, cultural values and everyday experiences.
This makes it important for Ghana to invest in the development and promotion of technologies that respond to local realities. AI should complement the country's educational objectives rather than introduce external solutions that may not adequately address local needs.
Responsible governance, ethical standards and effective data protection measures must therefore form an essential part of Ghana's approach to integrating artificial intelligence into education.
National Education Week 2026 is expected to provide an important platform for bringing these issues together and translating discussions into practical recommendations.
The two-day event will attract a broad range of stakeholders, including policymakers, teachers, school administrators, researchers, academics, student bodies, development partners, civil society organisations, technology providers and traditional authorities.
The opening day will feature statements on the state of education in Ghana, the commissioning of an exhibition showcasing digital education initiatives and technical presentations examining the current state of AI adoption and digital technology across the various levels of the education system.
The presentations will cover preschool, primary, junior high, secondary, technical and vocational education and training, complementary education, tertiary education and inclusive education.
A panel discussion will further provide an opportunity to examine global and African experiences and draw practical lessons for Ghana.
The second day will place greater emphasis on research and evidence, offering researchers and institutions the opportunity to present findings on AI adoption and digital education initiatives.
This focus on evidence is particularly important. Decisions about technology in education should not be driven solely by enthusiasm or the desire to appear technologically advanced. They must be informed by research, practical implementation experiences, measurable outcomes and a clear understanding of the challenges confronting educational institutions.
Technical group discussions will also allow participants to identify priority areas for action and develop recommendations to guide policy and implementation.
Among the expected outcomes are policy recommendations aligned with Ghana's national development agenda, a proposed National AI in Education Roadmap for 2027–2030, stronger partnerships among government and other stakeholders, and an ethical guidelines and data privacy framework for AI in pre-tertiary and tertiary institutions.
A draft 2027 Joint Sector Performance Aide-Mémoire is also expected to capture priority commitments on AI and digital technology.
These are important ambitions. However, their true value will depend on how effectively the recommendations are implemented, monitored and sustained beyond the event.
Transforming Ghana's education system through artificial intelligence cannot be the responsibility of the Ministry of Education alone.
Government must provide the policy direction, infrastructure and enabling environment. Educational institutions must be willing to embrace innovation while maintaining academic standards. Teachers must receive the necessary support and training, while parents must understand the changing learning environment and guide their children in using technology responsibly.
The private sector also has an important role to play in developing relevant solutions, supporting innovation and investing in digital infrastructure.
Development partners, research institutions and civil society organisations must contribute their expertise, evidence and resources to ensure that the transition is inclusive and sustainable.
Students, too, must be active participants. Beyond learning how to use AI applications, they must understand how the technology works, question the information it produces, recognise its limitations and apply it responsibly.
This calls for a broader understanding of digital education, one that places human development, intellectual independence, creativity and ethical responsibility at its centre.
As Ghana prepares for National Education Week 2026, the conversation must extend beyond the technology itself. The more important consideration is the kind of education system the country wants to build and the opportunities it hopes to create for the next generation.
A successful AI-driven education system must be one in which a child in a rural community has a meaningful opportunity to benefit from technological advancement; a teacher is empowered rather than displaced by innovation; a learner with a disability can access appropriate learning support; and a university student can use technology to explore new ideas, advance research and contribute to national development.
It must also be a system that protects learners, respects their privacy, promotes responsible innovation and recognises that technology is only as valuable as the human purpose it serves.
National Education Week 2026 therefore presents Ghana with an opportunity to align its educational ambitions with the realities of a rapidly changing world.
Its success will not be determined by the number of presentations delivered, the technologies displayed at exhibitions or even the policies developed. It will ultimately be judged by whether the recommendations lead to better teaching, improved learning outcomes, stronger educational institutions and more equitable opportunities for every Ghanaian child.
Artificial intelligence may be shaping the future of education, but the responsibility for determining that future rests with people.
Ghana must not simply prepare its learners to live in an AI-driven world. It must equip them with the knowledge, skills and confidence to shape that world.
